summary_notes.overview: A matrix is simply a neat, rectangular grid of numbers or functions arranged in rows and columns. It helps us organize data, like tracking how many notebooks and pens different people have, in a structured way.

core_concepts.title: What is a Matrix?
core_concepts.detail: A matrix is an ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions. Think of it as a table where the data is neatly lined up in rows (horizontal) and columns (vertical).

core_concepts.title: Elements (Entries)
core_concepts.detail: The individual numbers or functions inside the matrix are called elements or entries. For example, in the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 15 & 6 \\ 10 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, the numbers $15, 6, 10,$ and $2$ are the elements.

core_concepts.title: Rows and Columns
core_concepts.detail: Rows are the horizontal lines of elements, and columns are the vertical lines of elements. The size of a matrix is described by the number of rows followed by the number of columns (e.g., a $2 \times 3$ matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns).

core_concepts.title: Notation
core_concepts.detail: Matrices are usually denoted by capital letters like $A, B, C$. The elements are often written with square brackets $[\ ]$ or parentheses $(\ )$.

key_definitions.definition: An ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions.
Each individual number or function in a matrix.
A horizontal line of elements in a matrix.
A vertical line of elements in a matrix.

high_yield_takeaways: A matrix is just a structured table of numbers or functions.
The order of elements matters, so it is called an 'ordered' array.
Matrices can contain numbers, variables, or even functions like $\sin x$ or $\cos x$.
The size of a matrix is always written as (rows) $\times$ (columns).
Square brackets $[\ ]$ are the most common way to write matrices.

governing_formulas.name: Matrix Size Notation
governing_formulas.note: $m$ is the number of rows, and $n$ is the number of columns.

governing_formulas.name: General Matrix Form
governing_formulas.note: $a_{ij}$ represents the element in the $i$-th row and $j$-th column.

exam_traps.trap: Confusing rows and columns when stating the size of a matrix.
exam_traps.remedy: Always remember: Size = (Rows) $\times$ (Columns). Count the horizontal lines first, then the vertical lines.

exam_traps.trap: Thinking matrices can only contain numbers.
exam_traps.remedy: Matrices can also contain variables, functions, or even other matrices. Just keep the rectangular shape!

quick_quiz.explanation: A matrix is specifically an ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions. The order and rectangular shape are key.

quick_quiz.explanation: The size of a matrix is always written as (number of rows) $\times$ (number of columns). So, 3 rows and 2 columns means $3 \times 2$.

summary_notes.overview: A relation between two sets $A$ and $B$ is any collection of ordered pairs from $A\times B$. A function is a special relation where each element of $A$ appears exactly once as the first entry.

core_concepts.title: Relation
core_concepts.detail: A relation $R$ from $A$ to $B$ is a subset $R\subseteq A\times B$. If $(a,b)\in R$, we write $a\,R\,b$.

core_concepts.title: Function
core_concepts.detail: A function $f\colon A\to B$ is a relation where every $a\in A$ is paired with exactly one $b\in B$.

core_concepts.title: Domain, Codomain, Range
core_concepts.detail: Domain is the set of all first elements, codomain is the set $B$ we map into, and range (image) is the set of all second elements actually used.

key_definitions.definition: $A\times B$ is the set of all ordered pairs $(a,b)$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$.
An ordered pair $(a,b)$ keeps the order; $(a,b)\neq(b,a)$ unless $a=b$.
A function that has a reverse mapping $f^{-1}$, possible only when each $b$ in the range comes from exactly one $a$.

high_yield_takeaways: A relation is just any set of ordered pairs from $A\times B$.
Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function.
For a function, each element of the domain appears once on the left side.

governing_formulas.name: Relation definition
governing_formulas.note: $R$ contains the pairs that satisfy the given rule.

governing_formulas.name: Function definition
governing_formulas.latex: $f\colon A\to B\;\text{with}\;\forall a\in A,\;\exists!\,b\in B:\;(a,b)\in f$

exam_traps.remedy: Check if every element of the domain has exactly one partner; if not, it’s only a relation.

exam_traps.trap: Ignoring the order of the pair.
exam_traps.remedy: Remember $(a,b)$ is different from $(b,a)$; always write the first element from the domain set.

quick_quiz.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes a function?

options.text: Each element of the domain is paired with exactly one element of the codomain.
A function can pair one domain element with many codomain elements.
A function is any subset of $A\times B$.
The order of elements in a pair does not matter for a function.

quick_quiz.explanation: A function must assign one and only one output to each input; options B, C, D describe relations or incorrect ideas.

quick_quiz.question: If $R\subseteq A\times B$ contains the pair $(a,b)$, what can we say?

options.text: $a$ is related to $b$ under $R$.
$b$ is related to $a$ under $R$.
Both $a$ and $b$ belong to the same set.
The pair $(b,a)$ must also be in $R$.

quick_quiz.explanation: By definition, $(a,b)\in R$ means $a\,R\,b$. The relation does not automatically include $(b,a)$.

topic_study_top_chap_book_c12_phy_2026_1.topic_title: Fundamentals of Electric Charge & Coulomb's Law

summary_notes.overview: Electric charge is a tiny, quantised property of particles that can be positive or negative. Like charges push each other away, while opposite charges pull together.

core_concepts.title: Electric Charge
core_concepts.detail: Charge is a scalar quantity that can be positive (protons) or negative (electrons). It is always a multiple of the elementary charge $e = 1.602	imes10^{-19},	ext{C}$, written as $q = ne$ where $n$ is an integer.

core_concepts.title: Coulomb’s Law
core_concepts.detail: The force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: $F = k,dfrac{|q_1q_2|}{r^2}$, where $k = 8.99	imes10^9,	ext{N m}^2	ext{/C}^2$.

key_definitions.definition: The smallest unit of electric charge, carried by an electron or a proton.
Two charges of the same sign that repel each other.
Two charges of opposite sign that attract each other.
Charge can only exist in whole multiples of the elementary charge.
The total charge in an isolated system never changes.

high_yield_takeaways: Charge is always an integer multiple of $e$.
Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
Charge is conserved in any closed system.

governing_formulas.name: Charge quantisation
governing_formulas.note: $n$ is an integer, $e$ is the elementary charge.

exam_traps.trap: Mixing up the sign of charge with its magnitude
exam_traps.remedy: Always write the sign separately from the magnitude, e.g., $q = +3e$ or $q = -2e$.

exam_traps.trap: Forgetting the $r^2$ term in Coulomb’s law
exam_traps.remedy: Remember the force falls off with the square of the distance.

quick_quiz.question: Which of the following is true about electric charge?

options.text: Like charges attract each other.
Unlike charges repel each other.
Charge is a vector quantity.
Charge is always conserved in an isolated system.

quick_quiz.explanation: Charge is a scalar that is conserved in any closed system, so option D is correct.
